data.title: AfD surge in eastern Germany makes some immigrants question whether they still belong
data.description:
AfD surge in eastern Germany makes some immigrants question whether they still belong

By Amina Ismail and James Mackenzie
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 6:03 am UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Rostock before the state elections

1 of 3
Shahad Najeeb, 38, from Iraq, speaks next to her children, Zaid, 4, and Khaleed, 7, and her husband, Mahmoud Hmouech, 47, from Syria, in their apartment in Rostock's Luetten Klein district ahead of the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state elections, Germany, September 17, 2026. REUTERS/Annegret Hilse

By Amina Ismail and James Mackenzie

ROSTOCK, Germany, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Shahd Najeeb still remembers the trauma of fleeing Islamic State fighters during Syria's civil war. More than a decade after finding refuge in Germany, she now fears she may no longer be welcome there.

"When I think about the time we left Syria, I still don't know how we managed to get through it," she told Reuters in her ‌home in Rostock, on Germany's Baltic coast. "It was like a nightmare."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Najeeb and her husband, Mahmoud Hmouech, fled their home in Deir al-Zor in eastern Syria and rebuilt their lives in Germany, where he works in a ‌barber shop and she serves meals in local schools. They have two young children.

"We are grateful to the German people for welcoming us and giving us peace and security," Hmouech said. "The work we do is a small way of showing our gratitude."

They are among more than 900,000 Syrians living in ​Germany, most of whom arrived as asylum seekers during the civil war.

But as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) gains support and migration returns to the centre of political debate, migrants say hostility towards foreigners is growing.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Reuters spoke to 20 people of migrant background in Rostock and the nearby city of Schwerin, many of whom have become German citizens and have lived in Germany for years.

Most said they had encountered more anti-immigrant abuse in recent years, ranging from muttered remarks to demands that they return to their countries of origin. One woman said a neighbour poured foul-smelling water on her from a balcony.

Their concerns come as the AfD gains momentum across eastern Germany.

In Najeeb and Hmouech's home state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, in the formerly communist east, opinion polls suggest the AfD ‌is set to become the biggest party in an election on Sunday.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Earlier this month, the ⁠party, which wants to restrict immigration and talks about "remigration" - or sending foreigners back to their home countries - won its first major regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, another eastern state.

Several interviewees, including people working in healthcare, tourism, education and food services, said they would consider leaving Rostock or Schwerin if the climate continued to worsen.

'THIS COUNTRY IS FOR GERMANS'

Sitting in the family's small apartment in ⁠northern Rostock, where their children's drawings cover one wall and toys are neatly stacked in corners of the living room, Najeeb spoke as her children, aged 6 and 4, played nearby.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Najeeb, who studied physics in Baghdad and later worked as a jewellery designer in Syria, recalled stopping at a grocery store after collecting her children from school when, she said, an elderly man in a wheelchair shouted that she did not belong in Germany.

"This country is for Germans," he yelled.

"The pain I experienced in Rostock is a new kind of pain that ​I ​have never felt before," Najeeb said.

"You feel the injustice because you have done nothing wrong. I worked hard to build a life for ​myself and then someone comes along and treats you like garbage," she said, her voice ‌cracking.

She recalled her son asking: "Mama, why is he insulting you? What did you do to him?" Unsure how to explain, she told him the man was perhaps unwell.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

LABOUR FORCE

The AfD began as a eurosceptic party in 2013 and its anti-immigrant tone sharpened markedly after former Chancellor Angela Merkel's decision in 2015 to open Germany's borders temporarily, admitting around one million migrants and refugees, around a third of them Syrians fleeing the civil war.

Since then, it has grown from a fringe movement into Germany's most popular party, leading Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives in national polls.

Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD's main candidate in Sunday's election, says he has "absolutely no objection" to immigration by skilled workers. He says those who should be deported are the more than 250,000 foreigners who have no legal right to stay in Germany.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But critics say the broader problem is the atmosphere created by rhetoric they say targets foreigners in general.

During a televised debate on Wednesday, Social Democrat state premier Manuela Schwesig accused the AfD of "causing ‌widespread fear with its statements on remigration and workers from different cultural backgrounds."

"I think it's terrible that people who work here, who make ​their contribution and pay their taxes and social security contributions, are afraid and don't feel at ease," she said.

During the debate, she and Holm ​took a question from a design engineer concerned at the risk of losing a valued Moroccan draughtsman because of ​the racist insults he said he encountered regularly on the street.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Holm said it was "naturally a shame that there's such a mood". But he blamed the government for allowing illegal immigration and failing ‌to deport more than a fraction of foreigners formally required to leave the country.

The debate ​carries economic implications as well.

Around 50,000 people with a migration background ​work in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Economists have warned that like other eastern states with low birth rates and an ageing population, it will need more skilled workers.

According to data from Germany's labour office, around 316,000 Syrian nationals - not including Syrians who have acquired German nationality - work in Germany, most in full-time jobs that pay social security contributions.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Their unemployment rate is above 30%, but data show the longer people stay, the more likely they are to ​find work. Figures from 2023 indicate that among those who have been in Germany for ‌seven years or longer, more than 60% have a job.

Many Syrians say they hope to return home if conditions improve. Others, including Najeeb and Hmouech, increasingly see their future in Germany.

Whether the AfD's rise ​changes that calculation remains an open question.

Hmouech says he does not want his children to grow up feeling rejected by the society they call home.

"At the end of the day, family comes first," he said.

(Reporting ​by Amina Ismail in Rostock and Schwerin, Oliver Denzer in Rostock and James Mackenzie in Berlin, Editing by Ros Russell)

data.title: Two men arrested by Singapore police after Italy busts international child abuse network
data.description:
Two men arrested by Singapore police after Italy busts international child abuse network

Laura Chia
Updated Sat, 19 September 2026 at 5:40 am UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE – Two men, aged 27 and 33, have been arrested by the Singapore police for possessing or gaining access to child abuse materials.

This follows the arrest of 17 people by Italian police in an investigation into an Italy-based international network that distributed child sexual abuse material online. The arrests were announced by Rome's chief prosecutor on Sept 17.

In response to queries from The Straits Times, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) confirmed on Sept 19 that they had received information from the Italian authorities on an operation targeting a Telegram group that was sharing child abuse material.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Following up on the information received, the SPF arrested the two men for the offence of possessing or gaining access to child abuse material.

The police did not state the nationalities of the men or if they are known to each other.

Investigations are ongoing.

In Italy, an undercover Italian officer gained the trust of the Telegram group's administrators, becoming a co-administrator and gaining access to its private channels, reported AFP.

The network was run by four Italians and a Swiss national.

The operation, named Fly Trap, led to a Telegram community called New Saga, which had more than 1,000 users worldwide and required payments in cryptocurrency.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Italian authorities identified 996 accounts linked to 98 countries and shared the information with foreign authorities, leading to a number of arrests.

In Singapore, those convicted of possessing or gaining access to child abuse material, and knows or has reason to believe that the material is child abuse material face five years' jail, and a fine or caning.

data.title: ‘No response’: Yoga Inc shutters SAFRA Punggol outlet, cancels classes at Our Tampines Hub
data.description:
‘No response’: Yoga Inc shutters SAFRA Punggol outlet, cancels classes at Our Tampines Hub

Ann Neo,Calista Wong
Updated Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:40 am UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE – Boutique yoga studio Yoga Inc appears to have shuttered, with some instructors informed on Sept 18 that operations have ceased with immediate effect.

According to its website, Yoga Inc, founded in 2013, has two outlets – at Our Tampines Hub and SAFRA Punggol.

In a note to staff seen by The Straits Times, Yoga Inc's management said the company "will cease operations with immediate effect".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The e-mail, sent on the night of Sept 18, stated that Yoga Inc "does not have sufficient funds" to make payments.

It added that the company was unable to provide a date by which outstanding amounts, including salaries and contractor invoices, would be paid.

Customers who spoke to ST said they had received no information about what would happen to their unused packages.

Checks by ST on the website on the morning of Sept 18 showed that classes at both locations had been cancelled.

When ST checked the website again at about 1.30pm, the class schedule page had been deleted, leaving customers unable to book classes.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Yoga lessons were also unavailable for booking on fitness booking platforms Mindbody and ClassPass.

SAFRA Punggol said in a Facebook post at 2.40pm that the outlet was "closed till further notice due to operational issues".

The lights were off and the door was locked when ST visited the Our Tampines Hub branch at around 5.30pm.

But there were no visible notices about the studio's closure.

As at 2pm on Sept 18, the company's Instagram account had been deleted. Its final post, dated July 6, advertised a 10-class package for $210.

In response to queries, Yoga Inc founder Ashly Lo, who no longer owns the business, said instructors she had worked with were informed of the closure on the morning of Sept 18.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Founded in 2013 by Lo, Yoga Inc expanded to six outlets across Singapore at its peak, employing more than 30 instructors.

Lo, who ran the business on her own, told ST that she became exhausted and had sold the company to another instructor in February 2021. She did not say to whom she sold it.

She added that Yoga Inc had since been resold to a company that owns indoor cycling studio Revolution.

Phone calls by ST to both of Yoga Inc's outlets went unanswered on the afternoon of Sept 18.

Records from the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority show that Yoga Inc was struck off the register on Oct 6, 2025.

Customers not informed by studio

Edric Liew, a 36-year-old freelance instructor who taught at Yoga Inc for more than 10 years, said he had yet to be paid for August.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Another instructor, who has been with the studio for more than three years and did not want to be named, also said she had not received her August pay, which is usually sent out on the 15th of every month.

Liew added that the company did not inform customers of the closure and that they learnt about it only from their instructors.

"I feel sorry for the students... there was no lead time," Liew said. "They did not have time to finish their packages, and now management is uncontactable."

According to Liew, one class at 9.15am had taken place at the Tampines outlet on Sept 18, but all other classes have since been cancelled.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Angela Moghe, a customer who had been practising yoga at Yoga Inc for more than two years, said the studio did not contact her despite her having a noon class scheduled for Sept 19.

"I e-mailed yesterday, but there has been no response," the 57-year-old associate lecturer said.

Moghe had paid $405 for 20 classes in a special deal package bought in April. To date, she had attended only two classes, leaving her with 18 unutilised classes worth roughly $365.

She last attended a class on Sept 12 at the Tampines branch. There were no indications of an impending closure then, Moghe added.

Another student, who wished to remain anonymous, echoed the comments, saying that operations appeared to be running smoothly during her last lesson on Sept 14.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

She was not informed of the closure by the studio and only heard the news from friends who are instructors there, she said.

The student, who has been taking lessons at Yoga Inc since 2018, still has 19 unutilised classes in her pre-paid package worth $513.

Meanwhile, a 42-year-old student who declined to be named had 38 unutilised classes worth more than $1,000.

She originally had a class scheduled for Sept 18 at the Tampines outlet. But before the lesson, she received an e-mail notifying her that the class had been cancelled.

Still, she headed to the studio to check.

"When I went down, everything inside was still there as if it had just been closed for the day. No notification was pasted on the glass door," she said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Employees and customers ST spoke to also said that two other branches, in Tanjong Pagar and Bedok, had closed unexpectedly in the last few months.

The news comes after a spate of recent fitness chain shutdowns.

Earlier in September, customers and employees of True Fitness and True Yoga were left in the lurch after the businesses unexpectedly shuttered. Many members were left with unused packages and services, reporting losses of more than $609,000.

Hundreds of employees and freelance instructors who worked for the True Group lost their jobs overnight.

ST has contacted Yoga Inc, the Consumers Association of Singapore, the Singapore Fitness Alliance, the Ministry of Manpower and the National Trades Union Congress for more information.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

  • Additional reporting by Anjali Raguraman

Source: The Straits Times © SPH Media Limited. Permission required for reproduction

data.title: Protesters form human chain at Kennedy Center after Trump threat
data.description:
Protesters form human chain at Kennedy Center after Trump threat

Elodie SOINARD
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 5:28 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Protesters formed a human chain on Friday around the Kennedy Center, the Washington arts hub that US President Donald Trump threatened to demolish unless his name is restored to it.

The complex's main building has been shuttered since Wednesday -- temporarily, according to its leadership -- while a judge is also reviewing plans for a long-term closure to accommodate Trump's desired renovations of the aging facility.

Crowds waved placards reading "hands off Kennedy Center" and broke out into song beneath the scaffolding and tarps that have remained in place since workers removed Trump's name from the building in June following a court order.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump took control last year of the Kennedy Center -- inaugurated in 1971 following the assassination of US president John F. Kennedy -- and has pushed for a major renovation, claiming the building had been left in a state of disrepair by previous leaders.

Like other projects around the US capital, the president has shown an unprecedented keenness to put his personal touch on plans, while testing the legal bounds of executive authority.

Trump's handpicked Kennedy Center board voted last year to officially rename the institution as the Trump-Kennedy Center, with corresponding updates to building signage and online logos.

The move -- later reversed by a judge -- led to a major decline in ticket sales, artist boycotts and an exodus of donors, according to The Washington Post.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- 'Not a political place' -

"It makes me sick to my stomach," said Neal Racioppo, a Washington resident who runs marketing and communications for a theater.

Trump "can't get his name on this cherished building, so he is depriving the world of what it could be."

Racioppo, 57, joined a human chain that formed as night fell on the imposing, white, marble building, with crowds sprawling out onto the esplanade overlooking the Potomac River.

Demonstrators were zigzagged around the barriers installed after the center closed this week, with some waving placards reading "hands off Kennedy Center" and "Donny, you are no JFK".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It has been an important home for the arts for this city and this country and the world," Racioppo said.

"What President Trump is doing is despicable."

Lizzy Andrew, who has performed several times at the Kennedy Center, including singing with the National Symphony Orchestra, said she was angered at Trump's threat to tear down the venue.

"He does not have a right to decide that an institution, a living memorial to a past president, can be demolished," the 30-year-old told AFP.

"I think you can see tonight that the people of DC and the people of America do not agree with that decision."

Lela Agnew, who regularly brings her children to visit the center, said she came to defend an institution that "belongs to the people".

"I've been coming here for about 50 years," she said. "It's not a place that needs to be demolished."

"It's just not a political place."

data.title: Haze in Singapore: PSI in central region back in the unhealthy range
data.description:
Haze in Singapore: PSI in central region back in the unhealthy range

Laura Chia
Updated Sat, 19 September 2026 at 5:02 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE – The air quality in Singapore deteriorated on Sept 19 with the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) in the central region crossing into the unhealthy region again.

The 24-hour PSI reading in the area was 102 at 1pm.Air quality is considered unhealthy when the 24-hour PSI is in the range of 101 to 200, during which the NEA advises the public to reduce outdoor activities. PSI readings of 51 to 100 are considered moderate, while values of zero to 50 are in the "good" range.The hourly PM2.5 readings, which indicate the current concentrations of fine particulate matter, skyrocketed in the central region at 11am on Sept 19, moving from 67 to 117.

It increased further to 149 at noon, before falling to 141 at 1pm.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

PM2.5 readings are considered elevated if they fall between 56 and 150, and high if they are between 151 and 250.The NEA has advised the public to refer to the hourly PM2.5 reading if they are considering immediate activities and 24-hour PSI one to plan for the day ahead.

The central region includes the Thomson, Marymount, Sin Ming, Ang Mo Kio, Bishan, Serangoon Gardens, MacRitchie and Toa Payoh areas, according to the NEA website.

The air quality had begun deteriorating late on Sept 18, with the PSI reading at 76 at 9pm before creeping up again overnight and crossing the 101 threshold at 1pm on Sept 19.

In its daily advisory on Sept 18, the NEA said smoke plumes from forest fires in Kalimantan were observed to be drifting towards Singapore. Some smoke plumes were also observed in southern Sumatra.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Dry conditions are forecast to continue over parts of southern Sumatra and Kalimantan and smoke haze might affect Singapore as the prevailing winds are expected to blow from the east-south-east or south-east.

The 24-hr PSI was forecast to be in the high moderate to low unhealthy range, added the NEA.

The PSI crossed into the unhealthy range two weeks ago, hitting 101 in central Singapore on the morning of Sept 4. In the days that followed, readings in the central, eastern and western parts of Singapore occasionally crossed into the unhealthy range.

September's developments mark the first time since October 2023 that the PSI in Singapore hit unhealthy levels because of haze, with the authorities earlier warning of the risk of haze between June and October as a result of warmer and drier conditions brought on by both El Nino and the Indian Ocean Dipole.

Source: The Straits Times © SPH Media Limited. Permission required for reproduction

data.title: Cyclist, 16, arrested after accident with 74-year-old pedestrian who later dies
data.description:
Cyclist, 16, arrested after accident with 74-year-old pedestrian who later dies

Laura Chia
Updated Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:25 am UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE – A 16-year-old cyclist has been arrested for a rash act causing death following an accident involving a 74-year-old man.

The police said they received a call for assistance at Block 741 Yishun Avenue 5 at 11.45am on Sept 15.

The Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) took the man, who was a pedestrian, to Khoo Teck Puat Hospital where he later died, said the police.

The male teenager was arrested for the offence of rash act causing death and investigations are ongoing, added the police.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A man who said he is the 74-year-old's son, made an appeal for eyewitnesses on Facebook on Sept 16.

Tan Bo Xue identified the elderly man as his father, Tan Liang Kwong. He later said that his father had died on Sept 17. He said the accident took place near a Jollibee outlet in a Caltex petrol station located near the junction of Yishun Avenue 5 and Yishun Street 11.

Block 741 Yishun Avenue 5, where the police were called, is opposite the petrol station.

Tan also thanked a passerby, whom he says called the ambulance for his father, and asked the passerby to contact him.

data.title: Frustration grows as Houthis widen Middle East conflict with US unwilling to intervene
data.description:
Frustration grows as Houthis widen Middle East conflict with US unwilling to intervene

Kylie Atwood, Jennifer Hansler, Zachary Cohen, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:00 am UTC
9 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Dramatic recent advances by the Iran-backed Houthis, including the seizure of a strategically important island in the Red Sea, have dealt another blow to a region reeling from the US war with Iran and exacerbated an already severe global energy crisis. But neither the US nor its key ally Saudi Arabia has a clear plan to beat back the group, multiple sources told CNN, leading many in the region to ask where the counteroffensive will come from.

Although US officials acknowledge the Yemeni rebel group is advancing with the goal of ultimately asserting control over the critical Bab al Mandeb Strait, the Trump administration is signaling it has little interest in using the American military to stop them – relying instead on Saudi Arabia to do so.

But even with additional US intelligence and targeting support, Saudi Arabia has not been able to effectively stop the Houthis from taking key coastal towns in Yemen, frustrating Gulf and American officials. Sources who spoke with CNN expressed doubt that the Saudis would be able to stop the Houthis on their own.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Houthis moves have not come as a surprise to sources in the region, as well as former diplomats, who said the weaknesses of the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces were well-known. For months US intelligence reports indicated the group would attempt to close another key waterway for commercial shipping as Iran did earlier this year, US officials said.

Still, the US believes it is currently providing Saudi Arabia with everything it needs to be successful against the Houthis, one American official told CNN, referring to the recent increase in sharing intelligence support and sharing of targeting data support with the Kingdom. And after about a decade of training the Yemen government's military, the Kingdom had assured US officials that they were confident in their ability, two sources told CNN.

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces started fighting the Houthis, who are supported and trained by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), more than a decade ago during Yemen's brutal civil war. A 2022 UN-brokered truce had brought a period of relatively low levels of hostilities between the two sides.

However, the fighting has resumed and intensified in recent weeks. The Saudis accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca, Islam's holiest city, and the Houthis claim to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

President Donald Trump has made clear that his current red line is direct US participation in kinetic strikes against the Houthis. To date, US military support has been strictly providing intel and targeting data for Saudi strikes.

"No offensive strikes," said a US official.

'The Houthis called us and they don't want to fight'

Multiple Gulf and US sources say messaging from Trump signals to the Iranians he is unwilling to back US allies in the region.

"The Houthis called us and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said in remarks to reporters in Ireland last weekend. "They don't want us to go after them and would much prefer not having us involved and they're letting most ships go through."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It's just one country they're not too happy with," Trump said, referring to Saudi Arabia, "and we'll get that straightened out."

Barbara Leaf, a former US diplomat who worked throughout the Middle East called Trump's own comments about the Houthis "shocking."

"It's a pretty harsh way to treat your relationship with a close partner, to appear to privilege your agreement with a group you've designated as an (foreign terrorist organization) that attacked that partner," she told CNN. The administration designated the Houthis as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in March 2025.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice with Trump last week to ask for US strikes against the Houthis. That request, so far, has been rebuffed and sources said it is hard to tell if the administration policy will shift.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Amid this frustration over the Houthis advances, many Gulf sources believe the offensive represents a new front in the Iran war that could prolong the conflict. Despite some efforts to deal with the issues separately, sources increasingly believe there is unlikely to be progress on Iran without dealing with the Houthis.

"The Houthis' Red Sea push is emboldening the IRGC. The Saudis have to get this fixed, otherwise they are negotiating with a gun on the table and they won't do that," said Joey Hood, a former US ambassador who spent much of his career working in the Middle East.

Hood, like other sources, noted that although the Houthis claim their fight is just with Saudis, there is a clear nexus to Iran.

"Iran is in an existential battle now and pulling on all of their proxies to fight. The Houthis are not remote-controlled by Iran but they need fuel from them. So, the Houthi statements of why they are carrying out this offensive now are not a complete reflection of reality," said Hood.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The situation in Yemen has complicated the other negotiations, including those over the Strait of Hormuz.

A first meeting between Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and Iran since the US-Iran war began was canceled earlier this week. Saudi Arabia decided not to attend amid concerns around the language of a potential agreement between Oman and Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz and other Gulf countries followed suit. Regional sources said it was a clear signal that the Kingdom sees no upside to engaging with the Iranians amid active Houthi attacks.

"Due to the Houthi attacks and the situation near the Bab-el-Mandeb corridor, it's affecting the Strait of Hormuz deal," a regional source told CNN. "The Saudis are demanding an all-or-nothing approach, which is understandable, but it delays the process."

'No one wants to fight alone'

For about a decade, the Saudis have been training Yemen's military, and so far, those forces have been unable to effectively push back the Houthis. Saudi strikes, backed by US intelligence and precision targeting, have prevented the militia from exercising a firm command over some of the territory they have taken, but advances have not been wholly rebuffed.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The highest levels of the US government largely ignored the Houthi threat over the last decade despite lower-level US officials and regional players urging closer attention to the rebel group as it grew stronger, sources said. Last year's US military campaign against the Houthis also laid bare the limits of American firepower – as months of bombing failed to effectively dislodge the group's foothold inside Yemen and ended with an abrupt US-Houthi ceasefire.

The US "solidified the ceasefire" with the Houthis during a meeting in Oman this weekend, the US official said – a message that underscores the administration's unwillingness to get involved.

"The Americans sent a message," a senior Houthi official familiar with the matter told CNN Thursday, "that they don't want to join the Saudis and be part of the conflict."

"We received this message positively," the source added.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

There was a perception that Saudi Arabia's own firepower coupled with its investment in Yemen's military could counterbalance the Houthis' offenses, some current and former US officials say. That expectation has not panned out.

Others say the Houthi successes are hardly surprising, especially given unity of the militia and Iran's support.

"The Houthis have the advantage of having this really deep and productive relationship with the (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) which has trained them and taken them up several notches from the hard-scrabble kind of cave fighters that they were 12 years ago to a force that can really be quite devastating," said Leaf, who was a former Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs.

"The Houthi have spent a lot of time in the last months preparing their forces for just this kind of move," she continued. "They punched through the Saudi-aligned and Yemeni government-aligned forces, not surprisingly, just punched through them – the forces just disintegrated."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"No one wants to fight alone," said a current Gulf official. "Either the Saudis fight or they cut a deal with the Houthis."

But as it becomes clear that the Saudi-backed government will need more resources to take on the Houthis, the kingdom is also spread thin as they manage a wide array of challenges resulting from the ongoing war: a recent strike on their East-West pipeline, working with the US military on enabling tanker traffic through the strait, and keeping open a land-bridge to move critical resources through the region.

Saudi Arabia also cut oil exports to Europe for the month of September in recent days, triggering a recognition that the global energy crisis could deepen.

An effective pushback at the hands of Saudi-backed forces in Yemen is likely to require additional boots on the ground from Saudi Arabia or elsewhere, and a projection of commitment from the US, sources said. But neither of those inputs seem likely.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"At least the possibility of US involvement needs to hang over everyone to act as a deterrent, if you just unnecessarily wipe that away its demoralizing particularly to the Yemenis on the ground," another regional source said.

Leaf said she has not heard exasperation with the Saudis from officials in the region, but rather questions of "What the hell is the US going to do here?"

Gulf and US sources have also expressed doubts about whether the Houthi escalation can actually be entirely resolved militarily.

"They have been trying for years" to defeat the Houthis, the regional source said, noting that military action "will weaken them, yes, but will not end them."

CNN's Nadeen Ebrahim contributed reporting.

data.title: Within minutes: How quickly a scam site can be taken down under newly formed Cyber Command
data.description:
Within minutes: How quickly a scam site can be taken down under newly formed Cyber Command

Fatimah Mujibah
Updated Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:00 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE – If a website, phone number or social media page is linked to a scam, Special Constable Sergeant Javier Lau of the police's Cyber Command can take it down within minutes.

Previously, the process could take up to several hours, as Lau and his team would need to coordinate across multiple departments in the Singapore Police Force.

Lau, 22, a cybercrime operator and a full-time national serviceman, was among several officers from Cyber Command who spoke to the media on Sept 16, two months after the unit was launched on July 3.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

He said that when a site is reported, the team would assess whether it is malicious.

"We would document our findings and support follow-up actions that are required to disrupt the websites," he said. "The tempo is quick, especially during an active scam campaign. In those moments, we must work fast yet make sure that every case is thoroughly assessed."

Scam victims in Singapore lost $410.6 million in the first six months of 2026, with scam losses here hitting more than $4 billion since 2019.

In the first half of 2026, the police disrupted more than 47,000 scam-related mobile lines, 37,500 WhatsApp lines, 31,600 online monikers and 52,200 malicious websites.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

When asked about common scam trends, Lau said scammers often impersonate news outlets, including The Straits Times and CNA, to promote investment schemes and cryptocurrency sites to phish for contact information.

He said: "To the untrained eye, it can be quite convincing because it mirrors CNA and ST, but the content on the site is different."

When the site is assessed to be a scam, Lau and his team will contact the relevant internet service providers to take it down before more people are duped.

Said Lau: "This matters because scam websites can harvest victims' details within minutes of going live."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Assistant Superintendent of Police Nicole Morgan, 30, works with foreign law enforcement agencies and internal partners to fight cybercrime and scams.

She said Cyber Command helps with quicker decision-making.

Referring to a case in July, Cyber Command and the US Federal Bureau of Investigation prevented losses amounting to US$2.7 million (S$3.4 million) in the US and $388,000 in Singapore in a joint operation targeting transnational cryptocurrency scams.

The agencies identified 54 victims and potential victims of scams in both countries.

Morgan said: "Scam syndicates can move funds, change communications channels, replace infrastructure and relocate their members very quickly. For intelligence to be operationally useful, it must reach the correct agency and operational team in time for action to be taken."

She added that this can be challenging as every jurisdiction operates under its own legal and procedural framework.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

On Sept 9, the Scams (Countermeasures) and Other Matters Bill was passed, making it an offence to provide one's personal details to supply online accounts on Carousell, TikTok, Telegram and Meta's platforms to criminals.

Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs Goh Pei Ming had said then that the police receive an average of 90 reports of scams, involving about $2 million lost, daily.

He added: "Scammers will continue to adapt, and so must we. Our response must be sustained, coordinated and always forward-looking."

Lau said his work is meaningful as it has a direct impact on scammers.

He added: "Much of it happens behind the scenes, but acting quickly can shrink a scammer's window of opportunity and stop more people from becoming victims."

data.title: Defence firm Anduril says US delay on Taiwan arms sales affecting its business
data.description:
By Ben Blanchard

TAIPEI, Sept 19 (Reuters) - US defence tech firm Anduril's founder Palmer Luckey said on Saturday that President Donald Trump's delay in approving arms sales to Taiwan is affecting its business and that he ‌has discussed this with Trump.

The $14 billion package for Taiwan has been awaiting Trump's approval for months. After a ‌May summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump said he was holding it in abeyance and described it as a "very good negotiating chip".

China claims ​democratically governed Taiwan as its own, an assertion Taipei rejects. The issue of Taiwan is likely to be high on Xi's agenda when he meets Trump in Washington next week.

Speaking to reporters in Taipei where he attended a defence forum with Taiwan President Lai Ching-te, Luckey said he did not know the status of the arms package.

"It's definitely affecting the business in that our business ‌with Taiwan would be in a different place ⁠if you had that $14 billion moving forward," he said, declining to give details about what was being delayed for the company.

DRONES RESHAPE WARFARE

Anduril, whose Altius drone is used by Taiwan, has become ⁠one of Silicon Valley's hottest defence bets as drones reshape warfare in Ukraine and the Middle East and Trump pushes the Pentagon to adopt cutting-edge technologies to counter China.

Luckey, whom China sanctioned in December for selling weapons to Taiwan, said one of the problems in delaying ​the ​package was that it had a broader, longer-lasting impact. "It's that as ​long as that's stuck, you don't have continued forward ‌progress in other areas," he said.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside office hours.

China has repeatedly told the US to stop selling weapons to Taiwan and has sanctioned numerous US companies that sell arms to the island. The US is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, though Trump has called that commitment into question.

Luckey said he had discussed the issue of Taiwan arms sales with Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary ‌of State Marco Rubio. He said the administration was open to ​hearing from people on the issue but aware of the fallout that could ​come from selling more weapons to Taiwan, such as ​China using its leverage with rare earths crucial for tech companies.

"And so I've heard people say, ‌shouldn't he just approve the deal and damn the ​consequences? But he's getting briefed ​by other people who are not me, and they're saying, 'If you do this, here's what's going to happen to American consumers'," Luckey said.

"He has to weigh all of those things. He's in a really difficult, difficult situation," Luckey ​added, referring to Trump.

Lai, who shook hands ‌with Luckey at the forum's start, has made drones a central part of Taiwan's military modernisation.

Last year, Taiwan ​unveiled its first missile to be jointly made with a US company, Anduril's Barracuda-500, an autonomous, low-cost cruise ​missile.

(Reporting by Ben Blanchard in Taipei; Editing by William Mallard)

data.title: Cuba's electrical grid collapses again, plunging island into darkness
data.description:
Cuba's electrical grid collapses again, plunging island into darkness

By Dave Sherwood
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:24 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Cubans navigate shortages and power cuts in Havana

1 of 3
People walk along a darkened street during a power outage as a hotel remains illuminated in the background in Havana, Cuba, September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Ricardo Arduengo

By Dave Sherwood

HAVANA, Sept 18 (Reuters) - Cuba's electrical grid suffered a total collapse on Friday, plunging the nation into darkness and leaving ‌millions without power amid a US pressure campaign that has largely ‌blocked oil from reaching the Caribbean's largest island.

Friday's collapse was triggered by a failure in high-voltage ​transmission lines in central Cuba that occurred around 2 p.m. local time, authorities said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Protocols are now in place to begin the gradual restoration of the system," said Felix Estrada, an official with Cuba's National Electrical Union (UNE).

Power had returned to a ‌handful of scattered neighborhoods ⁠in Havana by late evening, primarily around hospitals, but much of the city remained completely dark under cloudy skies and ⁠rain.

The nationwide blackout, the latest of at least six partial or total grid collapses since January, hardly registered in a country accustomed to long hours, or even ​days, without ​power.

Many exhausted residents of the capital Havana ​were already without power when ‌the blackout hit.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Yesterday I'd gone without power for 24 hours. They turned the lights on for an hour, and then the grid collapsed," said Frank Lorenzo, a 23-year-old Havana resident looking forward to a long night of sweating and slapping mosquitoes.

Cuba's aging power generation system has been under severe strain from ‌fuel shortages and decrepit infrastructure for years, but ​a US-imposed oil blockade that began in ​January has vastly worsened blackouts ​and led to more frequent grid collapses.

The grid collapsed three ‌times in July and rolling blackouts have ​since spanned 30 ​hours or more across most of the country.

United Nations human rights experts have condemned the US oil blockade, calling it a violation of ​international law and warning that ‌Cuba risks becoming a "silent Gaza" as shortages and blackouts grow ever ​more critical.

(Reporting by Dave Sherwood, Ayose Naranjo and Alien Fernandez; ​Editing by Kylie Madry and Sam Holmes)
